analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Number 72 and 73, Stanislaw Nowak versus United States of America and Rebecca Misenberg versus United States of America. Mr. Goodman. Please, the court, these two cases are denaturalization cases. Both of them involve two aliens who were naturalized in the year 1938 in Detroit. And with respect to both of them, the cases were tried in the 1950s in Detroit before the same district judge. And in 1955, the opinions and judgments directing the cancellation of their citizenship was issued by the district court. In both cases, it is the government's claim that at the time and prior to denaturalization of Mr. Nowak and Mrs. Misenberg, they had been and were members of the Communist Party, which the government charged was an organization advocating the violent overthrow of the government, and that they knew and approved thereof. The pleadings, facts, and issues thus in both cases are the same, substantially the same, with one exception, which I'll mention. In the Novak case, the complaint was filed by the government under the 1940 Nationality Act. And under that act, and pursuant to its provisions, the government charged that Mr. Novak had obtained his citizenship through illegal procurement and by fraud. The Misenberg case was brought by the government under the 1952 Immigration Naturalization Act. And pursuant to the provisions of that act, the complaint charged concealment and misrepresentation of material fact. For the purpose of the argument, and because both parties have dealt at length with the issues in the case in the Novak briefs, I would like to, if court's permission, argue the Novak case until, at least until the court would like to have me mention something concerning the other case. I think that argument will dispose of, as far as I'm concerned, the major issues that are involved on this appeal. The facts in the Novak case, briefly, and insofar as they are material here, are as follows. Novak was born in 1903 in Poland. He came to this country at the age of 10, 1913. He has lived here ever since. In 1937, in Detroit, he filed his preliminary form for naturalization, as well as, later that year, his petition for naturalization. And following several interrogations by the immigration people, and after some investigation, in June of 1938, at Detroit, he was granted his citizenship upon taking his oath in open court. Within six months thereafter, in November 1938, he was elected from his district to the State Senate, or the State of Michigan, and was thereafter elected for five consecutive two-year terms, until 1948. In December of 1942, which was about four years after he had been granted his naturalization, the government obtained from the grand jury in the District Court of Detroit an indictment, a criminal indictment against Mr. Novak, charging him with having falsified during the course of his naturalization proceedings, swearing falsely. In that, the government at that time contended the indictment that he had concealed the fact that he was a member of the Communist Party, an organization which at that time, the indictment charge, was one which taught opposition to organized government. Several months later, in February 1943, the government, of its own motion, dismissed the indictment, and it was never reinstated. Approximately ten years later, December the 23rd, 1952, two days before the new 1952 Immigration Naturalization Act went into effect, this complaint was filed. The complaint was filed. The complaint was filed accompanied by an affidavit of a Ruben Spicer, which set forth what is alleged to be good cause for the institution of the proceedings. I will refer to the affidavit and my argument on that point. But the complaint charged both illegality and fraud by virtue of alleged membership in the Communist Party, an organization which the complaint at that time charged was one which advocated the violent overthrow of the government, and that he had knowledge of and approved of that advocacy. The case was tried. The government presented, I believe, twelve witnesses, two of whom testified concerning a claim of the government that he had falsified by denying membership in the Communist Party orally. However, the District Court, in its opinion, found that evidence to be insufficient and dismissed that allegation of fraud. The other witnesses testified as to the aims and objectives of the Communist Party introduced a number of books and literature which, however, were not attributed to the defendant, but in support of the so-called expert's opinion that they helped to fortify the expert's opinion that the Communist Party did advocate violence overthrow the government. A number of other witnesses testified that Mr. Novak had been a member of the Communist Party and attended meetings of the Communist Party and attributed certain statements to him, particularly three of the greatest importance in the government's case, which it is contended by the government and was found by the trial court to constitute advocacy on his part, or at least knowledge of the advocacy by the Communist Party, a violent overthrow of the government. And the court's opinion found that his citizenship should be canceled on the ground in both illegality and fraud. I would like to argue, insofar as I am to be able to, of course, in my argument, following three points. First, because it may be the jurisdictional question, one which the court may want to hear arguments, that the affidavit of good cause is insufficient in this case, under the ruling of this court in the Zucca decision. Secondly, I would like to argue that the charge of illegal procurement under the 1940 Act has no support and in any event is outlawed under the principle of race due to cotton. Third, I would like to argue that the claim of fraud, in the theory at least on which it is stated by the government in this case and upon which the evidence was produced, has not been proved. First, with respect to the affidavit. In order to discuss that, I want to just briefly refer to the Zucca opinion, which this court found that two things, as I read the opinion at least. One, that an affidavit was a prerequisite to the initiation of a proceeding of this kind. There being no affidavit in that case of any kind, the court's majority opinion held that the complaint should have been dismissed. And secondly, an ancillary holding in the opinion was that the verification of the complaint itself by the assistant district attorney, which was based upon an examination of the files in that case, was insufficient. It did not take the place of the affidavit which this court found was necessary to the maintenance of the proceeding. Now, the Spicer affidavit, that is the affidavit signed by Ruben Spicer in this case, which is the same practically in both Masonburg and the Novak case, and appears likewise in many of the other decided cases. This affidavit, the affidavit by Spicer, is an affidavit by the attorney for the Immigration and Naturalization Service. And the affidavit states that it is based upon an examination of the files of the service. This morning I had an opportunity of checking the records and briefs in the Zucka case, so this point is not in our brief. But in checking the complaint in the Zucka opinion, and comparing it in detail with the affidavit of Mr. Spicer in this case, the allegations are essentially the same, and the language is almost similar. Many of the paragraphs are exactly alike in specific language and specific allusions, and with respect to the formulations. For all practical purposes, a comparison of the complaint in the Zucka case and the Spicer affidavit in this case, I think will make it very clear that the affidavits, or the complaint and the affidavit, are practically the same. The comparison of the affidavit in both the cases before the court will indicate that it is essentially a form affidavit, or in the Zucka case, a complaint. So what we have here in connection with this issue, as we see it, is a question as to whether a sworn complaint as filed in the Zucka case, which was held to be insufficient by the court there, where treated in the same form as an affidavit attached to the complaint, would be sufficient, where in both instances it's based solely upon examination of the files and records. Now, in order to state our position on it, I would like to first indicate the extent to which I think the government misstates our position in its brief. They misstate our position, I think, because it makes it much easier to justify its own position. But their position argued for by the government in its brief is not our position. For the government there claims that what we assert and what we seek this court to do is that we claim, they say, that the affidavit must be, quote, the product of eyewitness observation, end quote. That's in the government's brief on page 47. We make no such claim, nor do we think that the court would be justified in holding the government to any such position. Our position, as argued in our brief and as it is here, is that the affidavit that's required by the government before it may institute a naturalization proceeding is one which is similar in nature to an affidavit which is required in order to obtain a search warrant or one that's required in order to justify extradition proceeding. Many decisions in both areas have pretty well made clear that in at least those fields, an affidavit which is required there is one which need not be based upon eyewitness observation. I think if any rule is to be applied to them, it's perhaps the one that's used by Wigmore extensively in his discussion of evidence. That is, there must be some circumstantial probability of the trustworthiness of the evidence set forth in the affidavit. I don't quote that from any decision of the court, but I think generally that is what the cases hold. It would, I think, be a rule that might well apply. In this court's decision in Zucca, you mentioned in the majority opinion an opinion issued shortly after the 1906 Act was passed by then Attorney General Bonaparte, which held, which was an opinion stating that a request for the institution of denaturalization proceedings requested from the department head in the form of an affidavit was sufficient to justify the institution of those proceedings. In its brief, the government here not only mentions that particular opinion, but at page 53 of its brief sets forth the letter from Mr. Strauss to the Attorney General, which he sets forth in detail the nature of the evidence presented as good cause for the institution of the denaturalization proceedings. Now, if the court will examine the Strauss letter, it is clear, I think, from the letter itself that what was submitted to the Attorney General as good cause was not a hearsay statement based upon examination of files such as is present in the Spicer Avenue. Rather, what was present there was a group of authenticated documents, copies of which were attached and duly authenticated, which set forth precisely and in detail and in the form of substantive original evidence the nature of the claim presented to the Attorney General that the alien in that case was over the age of 18 when he applied for citizenship contrary to the statute. So that if one were to compare that particular proceeding with the Spicer proceeding, one would have to say that Spicer should have, if his affidavit were to be based upon the same kind of evidence present in the other case, some original documentation or evidence which would have supported the ultimate conclusions which his affidavit consisted of. I further call the court's attention in this respect as an illustration of the kind of an affidavit which I think the government ought to be compelled to file if it wants to institute these proceedings. The case of Brinegar versus the United States. This is cited not in our brief but in the government's brief on page 65. This deals with search and seizure, not with denaturalization proceedings, but I think the principle is well stated there because in that case, which the government relies on, on the assumption that sufficient, an affidavit is sufficient which is based upon hearsay or at least non-eye witness observation, the court, this court said that the officers who made the search and seizure following an arrest without a search warrant in that case had personal knowledge and that search and seizure in that case were sufficiently based upon the personal knowledge of the officer. but in dealing generally with the problems of officers and connections with search and seizures, they make the observation that in dealing with probable cause, we deal with probabilities. And here, where good cause, which is tantamount to probable cause, I assume, we also can deal with probabilities. That does not mean hearsay conclusions by somebody who examines the file, but it deals more with, it deals with some basic facts, some basic information, some records, which the court can examine at the outset of the case and determine from his own observation on the basis of his own exercise of his own legal judgment whether, in fact, the material upon which the government relies for good cause justifies the conclusion that it is good cause. May I ask you, Mr. Goodman, whether affidavits by persons whose statements were in the Department of Justice filed on the basis of which the officer made the affidavits would have satisfied your criteria and your demands? If your honor means that if the affidavits filed with the Department of Justice had been attached, copies had been attached to Mr. Spicer's affidavits? Yes. Yes, I think that would have been sufficient because I think the criterion then would be, could the court, by examining the basic evidence which Mr. Spicer apparently examined, in examining this evidence have reached the same conclusion that Mr. Spicer did? As an illustration, the government in this case and this complaint charged not only the allegations I have mentioned but another one. They charged that Mr. Novak at the time he became a citizen owed his allegiance to the Soviet Union and that, however, because of his conduct and subsequent actions he did not disavow that allegiance and maintained his allegiance. Now no evidence was ever produced on that of any kind nor any claim made in part of it except what's in the affidavit. Whether there was any basis for that statement in Mr. Spicer's affidavit or not, nobody knows. Merely his conclusion. It may well be that there is nothing in the government's files which would permit the making of such a statement. Yet it appeared and no court could determine whether it was justified or not or gave rise to good cause or not unless you were to accept Mr. Spicer's affidavit that he examined the files and to him it appeared to be so. It ought not to be necessary though I find from time to time it is to say that questions don't imply any argument or agreement or conclusion so I'd like to put to you these questions. What this gets down to is that an affidavit by a government official that I have examined the file and I truthfully give the following hearsay a non-best evidence testimony as to what is contained in the file of the Department of Justice doesn't carry that weight which would justify a conclusion that he did that there are documents on file which he abstracted which he drew the meaning and that he fairly drew the meaning of things in the file isn't that right? That's what it gets down to. I'm not saying you're not right. No. Is that true? Is that a fact? I think that is true except I break it down to two points. The court in determining whether the affidavit is sufficient must first have the facts to decide whether there are facts claimed to be available. Then the conclusions to be drawn from those facts must be conclusions that the court may draw. In this case the court is in a position to determine neither one nor the other. No. Except that it has the assurance of a person carrying the authority and from my point of view impliedly the responsibility of the authority that I've faithfully given a break an abstract a summary of what I find in the file. You have that? That is there isn't it? And therefore the attack that you make or the inadequacy that you find is that it isn't enough to assume that a government official who makes such an affidavit authorized by some chief of the bureau whatever you call the deputy chairman of the deputy chairman of the deputy chairman A. that he's competent to make such a summary of what is in the files and B. that he's honest as well as competent. A. I should say that first that he's a man that he's not corrupt that he's trying to be honest in summarizing what is in the files and B. that he's capable of making such a summary. That's true isn't it? That's what it gets down to. His conclusions are substituted for the conclusions that the court would otherwise have to make himself from the facts. On the question of whether he has good calls. Yes. Now, with respect to the nature of the files themselves, I merely want to refer the court as an evidence of what such files might contain. Mr. Spicer in the affidavit refers to them of the official files. What he means by official is not clear and whether they are merely files that he has in his possession or files that the laws make official or not is not clear at all. But the nature of files in the hands of an organization of this kind of necessity and no criticism applied in it, but of necessity must be such as those which were described by J. Edgar Hoover in the Jenks opinion in the dissenting opinion by Justice Clark, which I think would, if transferred to the immigration department here, might well be, indicate that a person with the best intention might, from all the voluminous files which are there of the nature they're likely to be at, still present a conclusion which is not justified by the material which he has to go over. Well now let me ask you this in light of that. Glad you brought it out. Suppose the, suppose the affidavits were by people who were on the witness stand would be discredited in all sorts of ways. If these affidavits of the, if these affidavits of the primary informants were annexed, could the court say we don't believe them or we've heard or read or have a, a sufficient ground for believing that too many informants were not to be credited? Couldn't do that, could it? No. It would have to take the face value. However improbable the allegations may be. I think the Brinegar case answers that. There, the evidence on which the court found he had a right to make his search and seizure later was excluded at the trial on many reasons. The court said it does not depend upon whether it's admissible at the trial. It depends upon whether they are sufficiently probable so that at the time the affidavit is made the court can't give them credence. Now the, I just want to mention too that the government also infers to us the statement that what we require is an affidavit which contains the evidence in quote exhaustive detail. I merely want to say we make no such claim. We don't think it's necessary. A prima facie case is all that I think would be necessary in any event. I would think a prima facie case would have to be shown with respect to the facts of factual material. Now that does not mean that the affidavit may not refer to public records such as the judgment of naturalization or a petition for naturalization which might be in a public file. How many affidavits do you understand are permitted or at least required under this statute? I don't think any would be that there is any number required. I think the government says one affidavit. One affidavit. Well, when that's what the government argues that because the statute says it's on affidavit that means that it must be on one affidavit. I think that is a strange construction of the statute and I think that more than one affidavit might well be filed if the government wants to do so. Well, actually the word duty has some key significance in the first line of this statute. Does it not? I think it does. Might not a district attorney perform on his own the function of filing an information to punish the violation of the federal law? On his own now. And doesn't this statute seem to make it his duty to do so? His duty, whether he wants to or not, when an affidavit is filed. I think the court has held that the only way in which this procedure can be conducted is through the procedure set forth in the statute. By the filing of an affidavit and thereupon made the duty the district court attorney to proceed in the case. And the history of that statute I think reveals a reason why that procedure becomes necessary and why this court has held that it is a prerequisite. And in the Benzik case I think the court set forth there in considerable detail that only the procedure and only the procedure set forth by the statute is the one which can be followed in the denaturalization proceedings. I don't think that a district attorney may proceed under this statute on his own. Now, in the five minutes that are left to me I see that I'm going to be unable to discuss at all adequately the perhaps one of the most important aspects of this case involving illegal procurement. I do want to state one point in connection with fraud, however. Well, I may just briefly suggest under the on illegal procurement. The government's position on illegal procurement is that for five years prior to his naturalization he had been a member of the Communist Party and because of the organization which they claim it was and which they're supported by testimony introduced, therefore he could not have been and was not a person attached to the Constitution of the United States. I will not even touch upon the question of the sufficiency of the evidence. That's discussed at great length and I'll brief. But I do want to make this one point. The government claim, it is our main contention that the doctrine of the race judicata applies to the judgment insofar as attachment is concerned. And the government's main position on that is that because there are a number of cases decided by this court over a period of years which tell that under the claim of illegal procurement a naturalization judgment may be set aside such as a failure of certificate of arrival, no hearing in open court, racial ineligibility and so forth. Therefore, by the same token the judgment as to attachment may also be attacked on the ground of illegal procurement. It is our position that with respect to the matters that I have referred to in these other many decisions, these are jurisdictional prerequisites set forth in the statute which are readily ascertainable and which in the Baumgartner cases court held were specific conditions easily established whereas attachment is one which involves an ultimate judgment which is not of the kind encompassed in these decisions and therefore must be one which the court's opinion is final upon and may not be reassessed at a later date. I know I understand this. Inadequately discussed it. Are you saying that the court is final? The fact that the person has received a citizenship can't be re-canvassed? No, that isn't what I said. That's why I'm asking. What did you say? I said that the decision as to whether the person was attached to the Constitution is not the same kind of a decision as to whether he was, he had a certificate of arrival. As to the first, I think it is a judgment as to an ultimate fact which is final and which may not be reopened because of a doctrine erased to the court. What is final? I don't know. What is final? Well, nothing is final, I suppose, but in connection with the judgment of naturalization. Well, that's what I'm asking. When my father was naturalized, that couldn't be canvassed by any in a subsequent proceeding? Yes. Well, then what is final? The finality of the judgment, the judgment is final with the exception of fraud, common law fraud, and secondly, with regard to illegal procurement. Illegal procurement, we say, are the lack of the jurisdictional prerequisites to be exercised by the court of its power to act in such cases. One of those is not attachment because attachment is a final determination of the ultimate fact. That's what I mean. It is the determination that an alien who receives the judgment who obtained a favorable judgment, the naturalization involves a judgment, a judgment whereby he becomes a citizen. Is the question, the ingredients which led the judgment that he's attached conclusive and not reexaminable on the proceeding of the naturalization? Is that what you're saying? Well, certain of the agreement... I just want to know what you're saying. I say that... Not defended, just tell me what it is you're saying. A judgment of naturalization may be attacked in one of two manners under the 1940 Act, under the 1952 Act only in one way, but under the 40 Act in two ways. One, by fraud. We agree if there is a sufficient showing of fraud under the common law doctrines and under the doctrines applied by the court, you can take away a citizenship on that ground. But fraud with reference to his claim that he's attached, is that open? No. No, that is not. That's what I want to know. All right. Why isn't that? Because, as to fraud, the claim must be based upon a fraudulent... Well, I'm using the word fraud in my definition, but fraud itself must be a misrepresentation of a material fact upon which the government has relied upon, and it must be extrinsic rather than intrinsic in this nature. I was hoping that we were going to bury it. I hope so. I did not intend to come to it without some adequate preparation in my argument, but I finally got to it here. I'm through, but may I just... May I just ask you to be sure what it is we're considering. Do I understand that when a man's way is attached to the Constitution of the United States, and that oath, that affirmation, is accepted by a judge who looks him in the eye and says, this is an honest man. That is not the oath we're talking about. We're talking about the petition which he says he acts as a person who is attached for five years. That's different than the oath. That is required. The oath is in a different category. Well, he makes that allegation. That's right. Do I understand you that you can't show that in fact at the time he was a spy for a foreign government? And therefore not attached? I just don't... I didn't puzzle you. Well, he... As to whether he... I would say that there could not... On the question of attachment to the Constitution, that if he answered his questions correctly, and the prerequisites to the statute as to exercise of jurisdiction were all present, and he was granted his citizenship, later on, the court could not go back on a denaturalization proceeding and assert that during the course of those proceedings he was, in fact, acting as a spy and perhaps later convicted for it. Unless he were asked questions which related to it or unless Congress had put into the law a specific provision dealing with it. The question... Take the question of anarchists. Congress has put anarchists as a specific statement in the statute barring anarchists from being citizens. A person who is an anarchist may not become a citizen, and it makes no difference as to whether he is attached in fact or not because Congress has said so. There could be no element of racism in the statute that he owed but there may be racism in the statute of directions but the kinds of directions and that was the line up of the position of an hour. Yes, that's, I think, the position your honor took in his opinion in an hour. But we didn't go so far to say that the president was to show that he was sealed in court to justice frankly and the expression to the spy. No, I don't think the court came to that issue but when you put it that way... I understand that your views have some support in opinions expressed by individual members. I was wondering whether you're offering this thing as something justified by or confirmed by our opinion or something that you want the court, there being no quiet expression, to accept your view. No, I think that the point I am suggesting to the court here and the points we are raising here have been favorably passed upon by the court and certainly in the Schneiderman case with respect to the issues of evidence... That's a different story, the quantum of proof and on the Knauer case... Now whether the court intended in the Knauer case to apply the rule of race due to cop there, I believe, in my interpretation of it, that it did. I leave to the court itself the determination of whether it extrudes the decision that way or not. Before I sit down and through, I see by the light, but I wanted to just mention one point. In this brief on appeal, the government presents for the first time the issue of fraud in the oath. It was not presented by the government in the brief below. It was not argued by the district attorney in the court below. And therefore it was not argued or briefed by us at all in the court below or here. We find it for the first time here. We do not think it's properly in the case on appeal. If it is, we certainly don't think there is any evidence in this case to support it because of the post-naturalization record of this particular citizen, Mr. Novak, who was a member of the state Senate for five years, so completely opposite to that in Nauer, where that was the all-important consideration. But if the court does feel that that is an issue in the case at all, we would like to have an opportunity of filing a reply brief to answer, both because we don't think it's an issue and because we think the facts do not justify finding the fraud and will in this court for the first time. Mr. Bishop? May it please the court. Despite the fact that there have apparently been some narrowing of the issues to say nothing of concessions, I think that surely our discussion of the affidavit will be a cleaner and more easy to follow discussion if I divide it very sharply into two questions and devote myself first to the question as to who may make the affidavit. Somewhere in the petitioner's brief, there was the complaint of lack of personal knowledge and it was on that basis that we addressed ourselves for the question but it's a legitimate enough question of the court as well. So if I may, I want to warn the court that I'm going to try to narrow my discussion first to the question of who may make this affidavit. In other words, is it an insufficient affidavit because it is made by one who is not an eyewitness of everything. I'm concerned about that question as a remaining question as well because in the cases cited by petitioner in his brief by way of analogy in some of the search cases, there was an array of those earlier cases that not only said that it had to be on personal knowledge and an eyewitness but that it had to be by someone who would be legal evidence. Now those cases were the basis on the second round of some cases cited by petitioner and they have been, I think, very substantially overruled by Brinegar and the like. But in ascertaining what sort of an affidavit is intended here, I want to stay away, if I may, from the question of how much should he have said some more. Was this enough? I want to address myself first and clean up the question, I hope, in accordance with what I conceive to be the concession, but to be sure that the court has no lingering doubts about the fact that an immigration attorney, with the expertise to be attributed to him, and with some right to be considered honest and of some judgment, is a proper person to make this affidavit, although by the nature of the case he couldn't be an eyewitness to everything that occurred. Now there is a... Now, isn't that stated more broadly than the issue raised by the defendant could not be an eyewitness? Counsel said that he doesn't require him to be an eyewitness, and I thought he stated rather clearly what he thought would suffice. Well, first of all, I... I thought he said it was something like an affidavit for a search warrant or some other proceedings of that kind, which do not require a man to be an eyewitness to all these things, but it does require them to show probable cause. If I were clear that the court agreed, why then I could dispense with that part of the argument, but I'm afraid that the case is cited upon review in the brief, if I may take a little time to go through those, lest there be a lingering doubt, and also, because it will differentiate the questions of how much more, why wasn't this enough, how much should he tell? Now, that is narrowed, as I will note in that point of argument, that we need not fear that everything has to be put in. Now, with that in mind, I want to attack that personality problem, the person who is to do it in the orthodox way, first with a quick look at the statute, secondly with a look at the contemporary history, and so on down the line. As to the language of the statute, it says affidavit. Now, I don't want to put too much store on the fact that it says affidavit in the senior, but it is something of a benchmark that the Congress was not considering, the string of affidavits that would be necessary in a number of cases. what is more to the point is that draftsmen, when they do consider an affidavit that has to be on personal knowledge, can do so. Now, in the government's brief at page 49, we have set forth a sample of the type of draftsmanship which we think is indicated and indeed required if the ordinary definition of an affidavit is to be departed from.
